title: Exceptions in Pipelines
summary: Keeping exceptions precise once several instructions are simultaneously in flight, and the in-order commit trick that makes it possible.

slides.markdown:
In a single-instruction-at-a-time machine, an exception (divide-by-zero, page fault, invalid opcode) is simple: stop, handle it, resume. In a pipeline, several instructions are in flight at once — some older, some younger than the one faulting — and the hardware must still make it **look** as if execution stopped cleanly at exactly one instruction.

That illusion is called a **precise exception**, and it's what lets an OS handler, or a debugger, reason about program state as if the CPU weren't pipelined at all.

slides.subTitle: What "precise" means
slides.markdown:
A **precise exception** guarantees: every instruction before the faulting one has fully completed (all its state changes are visible), the faulting instruction itself has made no visible changes, and every instruction after it looks as if it never started.

This matters because OS exception handlers and debuggers need to inspect and resume state confidently — if instructions could complete out of the strict program-order boundary around the fault, the saved PC and register state might not correspond to any real point the program could have reached.

slides.subTitle: Exceptions surface late, at different stages
slides.markdown:
Different exception types are detected in different pipeline stages: an invalid opcode is caught in decode, an arithmetic overflow in execute, a page fault in memory access. So by the time a fault is confirmed, younger instructions (issued after the faulting one) may already be several stages further along — some might even be closer to completing than the instruction that's about to fault.

The pipeline must not let those younger instructions actually finish (write back their results) until it's certain the older instruction didn't fault — otherwise the precise-exception illusion breaks.

slides.subTitle: Flushing younger instructions
slides.markdown:
Once an older instruction's exception is confirmed, every younger in-flight instruction is flushed before its results become visible, and the PC redirects to the handler.

![Flushing younger in-flight instructions once an older instruction's exception is confirmed, then redirecting to a handler](assets/exception-flush-and-redirect.svg)

Same mechanism as a branch-misprediction flush: discard speculative work that must never commit.

assets.alt: Flushing younger in-flight instructions once an older instruction's exception is confirmed, then redirecting to a handler

slides.subTitle: In-order commit
slides.markdown:
The trick that makes precise exceptions tractable, even when detection happens at different stages for different instructions, is **in-order commit**: no instruction is allowed to make its result permanently visible (write back to architectural state) until every older instruction has already committed cleanly.

So even if a younger instruction technically finishes its computation earlier, its write-back is held until its turn — the moment an older instruction is found to have faulted, every younger instruction still waiting to commit simply never does, and gets flushed instead.

slides.subTitle: Two faults, one pipeline
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If two in-flight instructions both raise an exception, report whichever the hardware detects first."

**Why it's wrong:** exceptions surface in different stages, so a *younger* instruction (further along, say in MEM) might be detected before an *older* one (say still in EX) even reaches its own check. Reporting the younger one first violates program order — the program never validly reached that point.

**Correct model:** hardware must always report the **oldest** faulting instruction; the younger one gets flushed and re-executed after the older exception is handled.

slides.subTitle: Precise exceptions get much harder later
slides.markdown:
| | Simple in-order pipeline | Out-of-order CPU |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction completion order | Matches program order | Can differ wildly from program order |
| Precise exceptions via | In-order commit is nearly free | Requires a reorder buffer to fake in-order commit |
| Complexity | Low | Significant — a major design challenge |

In a simple in-order pipeline, in-order commit falls out almost for free since instructions already progress in program order. Out-of-order CPUs execute instructions in whatever order operands become ready, so they need dedicated hardware — a reorder buffer — purely to reconstruct the illusion of in-order commit for precise exceptions. That harder problem is covered in [Out-of-Order Execution](out-of-order-execution).
